messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan, a twenty-year-old aspiring writer, once held a vibrant, optimistic view of life, but that world shattered irrevocably six months ago with the sudden, unexpected death of his younger sister, Priya. One moment, she was laughing on the phone, telling him about her day at university; the next, a frantic call informed him she had collapsed, a previously undiagnosed heart condition claiming her life in an instant. This sudden, brutal loss utterly destroyed Rohan’s beliefs about how the world works, convincing him that life was an unpredictable, cruel lottery. He had come to believe that the world was an inherently dangerous place, where tragedy could strike anyone, anytime, without warning.

This profound shift in his worldview left Rohan in a state of perpetual dread. He was unable to relax, even in the supposed safety of his own apartment, his muscles constantly tensed, his senses on high alert. Any ordinary sound, like a car horn outside his window or a dropped pen, would make him jump or startle violently, his heart pounding as if in immediate peril. Sleep became a nightly battle; he would lie awake for hours, his mind racing, trouble falling or staying asleep a constant torment. Because he now truly believed the world was so perilous and that his own happiness was irrevocably lost, Rohan found himself unable to make any plans for the future. What was the point, he reasoned, if everything could be snatched away in an instant? He also began to actively avoid anything that reminded him of Priya, packing away her photos, changing the music they used to listen to, and even deleting old text messages.

His chosen profession, writing, became a minefield. The act of creating narratives, of imagining futures for characters, felt futile and dangerous. He’d stare at blank pages, unable to plot stories or develop characters, as if making plans for them was an act of tempting fate. This avoidance of future plans, coupled with his relentless efforts to avoid grief reminders, had unintended consequences. The more he pulled back from engaging with life, the more isolated he became, which only solidified his conviction that he was now a miserable person and that his happiness was truly lost. He found himself constantly asking his friends and family to reassure him that he was okay, but their words often felt hollow, leaving him feeling more fragile and reinforcing his belief that he was fundamentally broken and that the world was still too dangerous to navigate on his own.

This constant effort to avoid anything that might bring up painful memories or force him to consider a future without Priya kept Rohan in a perpetual state of hypervigilance. He was constantly scanning his environment for potential triggers, which made him even more unable to relax, as his nervous system was always on high alert. This constant monitoring exacerbated his sleep problems, as his mind couldn’t quiet down from the endless vigilance. The cumulative weight of these symptoms has become unbearable. Rohan now seeks help, desperate to understand why he feels so perpetually on edge, so hopeless, and what it would take to reclaim even a fraction of the peace he once knew. He fears he might never escape this suffocating cycle of dread and avoidance.
